g: flight time, how long will my drone fly, hover time, endurance, battery life drone
a: Flight time ≈ battery Ah × 0.8 (usable) ÷ average current × 60 min. Hover current ≈ (all-up weight in g ÷ 7 g/W) ÷ pack voltage for a typical quad (8–12 g/W for efficient long-range builds with big props). Example: 800 g, 4S 1500 mAh → ≈114 W, 7.7 A, ≈9 min hover, 4–6 min flying hard. Ask me: “flight time 1500 mah 4s 800 g drone”.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: thrust to weight, t/w, how much thrust, motor thrust, enough thrust drone
a: Total max thrust ÷ all-up weight. 2:1 is the minimum for stable, controllable flight (camera, mapping, payload); 3–5:1 for freestyle; 6–10:1 for racing. Hover throttle ≈ 1 ÷ ratio. Get thrust from the motor maker's test table for your exact prop and voltage.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

t: Choosing drone motors (KV and stator size)
g: motor kv, brushless motor size, 2306, 2207, motor sizing drone, kv rating
a: Stator size like 2306 = 23 mm diameter, 6 mm tall; bigger stator = more torque. KV = rpm per volt with no load: high KV for small props/low voltage, low KV for big props/high voltage. Typical: 5 in props on 6S → 1700–1950 KV 2207; 5 in on 4S → 2400–2750 KV; 7 in long range 6S → 1300–1500 KV 2806.5; 10 in+ → 400–900 KV.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: propeller size, prop pitch, 5 inch prop, 5x4.3x3, blades, prop selection
a: Props are named diameter × pitch × blades in inches (5×4.3×3). Larger diameter = more efficient thrust at lower rpm; more pitch = more top speed and current; more blades = more grip and current, less efficiency. Frame size sets max prop: about 5 in props on a 210–230 mm frame, 7 in on 280–320 mm, 10 in on 450 mm.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

t: LiPo battery C rating and cells
g: c rating, lipo, 4s, 6s, cells, max discharge, mah, battery current, lipo safety
a: Max current ≈ C × capacity (Ah): 1500 mAh 100C → 150 A on paper; real packs deliver maybe 60–70% of the label. Cell count S × 3.7 V nominal (4.2 V full, don't go under 3.5 V resting). Store at 3.8 V per cell, charge at 1C on a fireproof surface, and retire puffy packs.

g: esc, electronic speed controller, esc amps, 4 in 1 esc, blheli
a: Choose an ESC whose continuous rating is at least 20–30% above the motor's maximum current at full throttle with your prop (from the thrust table), and rated for your cell count. 4-in-1 boards are rated per motor. Use a low-ESR capacitor across the battery pads on 6S.

g: drone frame, quadcopter frame, arm thickness, carbon fiber frame, frame size, motor to motor, frame arms
a: Frames are sized by motor-to-motor diagonal (mm). Arms carry up to the full motor thrust as a cantilever: bending stress = 6·F·L/(b·t²). Racing frames use 4–6 mm 3K carbon plate arms (stiff so the PID loop isn't fighting flex); printed frames work for prototypes and small whoops but need much thicker arms. Keep the frame's resonance away from motor frequencies and soft-mount the flight controller.

g: drone payload, how much can a drone lift, lift capacity, carry weight drone
a: Usable payload ≈ (total max thrust ÷ 2) − all-up weight without payload, keeping 2:1 thrust-to-weight. Example: 4 motors × 1.2 kg = 4.8 kg thrust → up to 2.4 kg flying weight; with a 1.6 kg drone that leaves about 0.8 kg payload. Flight time drops quickly as weight rises.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: flight controller, betaflight, ardupilot, px4, inav, fc, gps drone
a: Betaflight: racing/freestyle quads, acro flying. INAV: fixed-wing and GPS hold/return on small drones. ArduPilot and PX4: autonomous missions, survey, rovers and boats, with full GPS, compass and telemetry. Mount the FC at the centre on soft grommets and match its gyro orientation in software.

g: faa drone rules, register drone, part 107, drone license, trust test, remote id
a: In the US: register drones over 250 g, take the free TRUST test for recreational flying, fly under 400 ft, keep line of sight, avoid controlled airspace without LAANC authorization, and broadcast Remote ID. Flying for pay needs a Part 107 certificate. Other countries have their own rules.

t: Servo torque for a robot arm joint
g: servo torque, arm joint torque, robot arm servo, kg cm, shoulder torque, how strong a servo
a: Holding torque = g × (payload mass × reach + link mass × reach/2 + next servo mass × its distance). The shoulder sees the most. 1 N·m ≈ 10.2 kg·cm. Choose a servo rated 2× the computed torque, since stall torque isn't continuous torque. Ask me: “servo torque for a 300 mm arm lifting 500 g”.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

t: Stepper vs servo vs DC gearmotor
g: stepper vs servo, which motor for robot, dc motor, gearmotor, bldc, nema 17
a: Steppers (NEMA 17/23): precise open-loop positioning at low speed, hold torque, but lose torque at high rpm and can skip steps; great for 3D printers and CNC. Hobby servos: cheap built-in position control over ~180°, good for small arms and grippers. DC gearmotors with encoders: efficient for wheels and continuous rotation. Closed-loop servomotors/BLDC: high speed and torque with feedback, best performance, most cost.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: nema 17, nema 23, stepper size, stepper torque, holding torque
a: NEMA size is the face width in tenths of an inch: NEMA 17 = 42.3 mm face, 31 mm bolt square, M3 screws, 5 mm shaft, roughly 0.3–0.6 N·m holding torque. NEMA 23 = 56.4 mm face, 47.1 mm bolt square, 6.35 or 8 mm shaft, roughly 1–3 N·m. Torque falls as speed rises; use the pull-out torque curve, not holding torque.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

t: Wheel drive torque for a robot
g: wheel torque, drive motor torque, robot motor size, rover motor, how strong motor for robot car, how fast will my robot go
a: Drive force F = m·(a + g·sinθ + g·Crr) (Crr ≈ 0.01–0.05 on hard floors, 0.1+ on grass). Torque per motor = F × wheel radius ÷ number of driven wheels. Wheel speed rpm = v ÷ (π·d) × 60. Add 1.5–2× margin. Ask me: “wheel torque for a 5 kg robot with 65 mm wheels”.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data
q: how fast will my robot go

g: tank tracks, treads, mecanum wheels, omni wheels, skid steer, differential drive
a: Differential (two driven wheels + caster): simplest and efficient. Skid-steer/tracks: best grip on rough ground and stairs but waste power turning. Mecanum/omni wheels: move sideways on smooth floors, poor on rough ground. Ackermann steering (like a car): efficient at speed, bigger turning circle.

g: pid, pid tuning, p i d gains, proportional integral derivative, oscillation, tune controller, my robot oscillates around the target, why does my drone wobble when i punch out
a: P reacts to the current error (too high → oscillation), I removes steady error over time (too high → slow overshoot and windup), D damps fast changes (too high → noise and hot motors). Tune with I and D at zero: raise P until it oscillates, back off ~30–50%, add D to damp overshoot, then add a little I to remove droop. Change one gain at a time and log the response.

g: gear ratio robot, gearbox, reduce speed increase torque, harmonic drive, planetary
a: Ratio N multiplies torque by N × efficiency and divides speed by N. Spur stage ≈ 95–98% efficient, planetary ≈ 90–97% per stage, worm ≈ 40–85% (self-locking, good for holding), harmonic/strain-wave ≈ 70–85% with almost no backlash. Pick N so motor rated torque × N × efficiency ≥ 2× required joint torque and output speed is still enough.

g: robot sensors, lidar, ultrasonic, imu, encoder, time of flight, distance sensor, imu for balancing robot
a: Ultrasonic (HC-SR04): cheap, 2–400 cm, wide beam, bad on soft or angled surfaces. ToF laser (VL53L0X/L1X): narrow beam, up to 2–4 m. LiDAR: 360° maps for navigation. IMU (gyro + accelerometer, e.g. MPU6050/BNO085): orientation and balance. Wheel encoders: odometry and speed control. Limit switches: homing. Cameras: vision with OpenCV/AI boards.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: robot controller, arduino vs raspberry pi, esp32 robot, ros, microcontroller for robot
a: Microcontrollers (Arduino, ESP32, Teensy, RP2040) run real-time motor and sensor loops. Single-board computers (Raspberry Pi, Jetson) run vision, mapping and ROS 2 but are not hard real-time, so pair them with a microcontroller for motors. Use dedicated motor drivers (TB6612, DRV8833 for small DC; TMC2209 for steppers; ESCs for brushless).

g: robot arm design, degrees of freedom, arm links, reach, payload robot arm, 6 dof
a: Keep heavy motors near the base and the links light and stiff; torque grows with reach squared once link weight counts. 4–6 DOF covers most pick-and-place. Add bearings at every joint so the motor only provides torque, not support. Use belts or rods to move motor weight back from the elbow, and counterbalance springs for the shoulder.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data

g: robot battery, power budget, power robot, voltage regulator, buck converter, how big battery robot
a: Add up average current of motors, servos and electronics; runtime ≈ Ah × 0.8 ÷ amps. Power servos from their own regulator (5–7.4 V, several amps); never from the microcontroller's 5 V pin. Use a buck converter for logic, a fuse on the battery lead, and a main switch. LiPo or Li-ion packs for weight; NiMH or lead-acid for cheap, safe benches.
s: rule of thumb; check maker data
